findings.source_quote: ...If I will that he [John] tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me. John 21:22.
findings.suggested_fix: Preserve the explanatory bracket around “John” (or reproduce its sense) in Arabic to mirror the author’s editorial note. For example: «فَإِنْ شِئْتُ أَنْ يَبْقَى هُوَ (يوحنا) إِلَى مَجِيئِي، فَمَا لَكَ؟ اتَّبِعْنِي. يوحنا 21:22.»
findings.translation_quote: «فَإِنْ شِئْتُ أَنْ يَبْقَى هُوَ إِلَى مَجِيئِي، فَمَا لَكَ؟ اتَّبِعْنِي. يوحنا 21:22.»

findings.location: Paragraph about 'ravening wolves' (near paragraph: “Now separated from its original identity as sheep...”)
findings.source_quote: Now separated from its original identity as sheep in this world, the coming centuries would see “Christians” become ravening wolves, destroying, killing, and corrupting.
findings.suggested_fix: The English phrase “ravening wolves” conveys the idea of predatory/rapacious wolves. The Arabic translation “ذئاب منكوبة” reads as “afflicted/stricken wolves,” which alters the metaphor. Use a term that preserves predatory sense, e.g. «ذِئابٌ جائعةٌ كاسرةٌ» or «ذئاب مفترسة».
findings.translation_quote: "الآن، منفصلة عن هويتها الأصلية كخراف في هذا العالم، ستشهد القرون اللاحقة تحول \"المسيحيين\" إلى ذئاب منكوبة، مدمرة، قاتلة، وفاسدة."

findings.suggested_fix: The translator uses inconsistent transliterations/forms (e.g. "أنابابتستيين", "الأنابابتست"). Use a single conventional Arabic form throughout (for example: «الأنابابتست» for the movement and «الأنابابتستيون» or «الأنابابتستيون/الأنابابتستيون» for people) to ensure clarity and consistency.
